items.name: Backpacks
items.fact: With nowhere to put what you own, everything is limited to what you can carry in your pockets and arms. Having something with a zipper minimizes spills and exposure to the elements.

items.name: Thermal socks
items.fact: Trench foot needs only about ten hours of wet at temperatures as mild as 55 degrees; a dry foot restarts that count.

items.name: Rain ponchos
items.fact: We get rain three out of five days in the PNW from November through February, and clothes that stay wet cost a body up to 40 percent more heat, enough for hypothermia at temperatures in the forties or fifties depending on the wind.

items.name: Beanies
items.fact: Hands and feet get shut down to keep the core warm; the head never does. A cover for the scalp and ears maintains both comfort and heat for the rest of the body.

items.name: Bivvies
items.fact: A mylar sack stops about 80 percent of the heat a body radiates during sleep, and one that folds back down and fits back in the backpack makes that true night after night.

items.name: Underwear
items.fact: Dermatologists warn that wearing the same pair too long raises the risk of irritation, bacterial growth and infection. A spare increases opportunities to keep one washed for replacement.

items.name: Gloves
items.fact: Warm fingers hold about twice the dexterity of cold ones.

items.name: Antifungal cream
items.fact: A damp foot grows fungus in days; getting rid of it takes a month of treating it.

items.name: Barrier cream
items.fact: Zinc oxide has been recognized by the FDA as a skin protectant against wind and cold. Reducing skin breakage is one of the only ways to prevent infections.

items.name: Wet wipes
items.fact: A moist towel can remove two thirds of dirt and grime in moments where running water is not in reach.

items.name: Toothbrushes
items.fact: Mechanical brushing is the only proven method to remove everything growing on teeth.

items.name: Toothbrush cases
items.fact: Stored anywhere, a barrier keeps dirt off bristles and anything on them off anything important.

items.name: Toothpaste
items.fact: Enamel doesn't grow back the way the rest of you heals — let decay take it and it's gone for good, so keeping your teeth comes down to keeping them clean.

items.name: Lip balm
items.fact: Lips have no oil glands of their own and dry out about ten times faster than the rest of the face, which is why cold wind chaps them first. An applied seal is among the best ways to prevent this.

items.name: Menstrual cycle support
items.fact: Without the products they need, people are forced to improvise with rags or toilet paper, which raises the risk of leaks and of urinary tract and other infections. Five days and nights of coverage, plus extra liners for spotting, helps reduce the month's risk.

items.name: Water bottles
items.fact: Dehydration sets in within hours and the body can't go more than a few days without water. Having a reusable container helps with knowing which one is yours, preventing leaks, and bridging the gaps between sources.

items.name: Peanut butter
items.fact: Few shelf-stable foods carry as much protein and dense energy ounce for ounce; one pouch holds 7 grams of protein with no preservatives. For those that can have it, a portable snack that tastes good can help with hunger between meals.

items.name: Apple sauce
items.fact: Nearly nine in ten adults fall short on fruit, and a diet of what keeps only widens the gap — a pouch of this is a full serving, no fridge or cooking.

items.name: Energy bars
items.fact: High-effort days leave the body hungry in between meals. A wrapped bar can be eaten anywhere energy or concentration are low.

items.name: Floss picks
items.fact: A brush never reaches between the teeth, where decay quietly starts — a handle gets in there one-handed.

items.name: Electrolyte sticks
items.fact: After hard sweat or a sickness, plain water alone won't always hold — it takes the salts the body lost to take the water back in.

items.name: Pain reliever
items.fact: Pain you can't treat wears down sleep and focus until getting through the day is the whole day — treating it early helps keep it from settling in.

items.name: Bandages
items.fact: A cut left open in the grime heals slow and invites infection; kept covered and moist, it stays clean and closes far faster.

items.name: Antibiotic ointment
items.fact: Cuts that stay dirty often get infected. An antibiotic can significantly reduce that.

items.name: Alcohol wipes
items.fact: With no sink in reach, nothing stands between hands and what they carry before eating or touching a wound — a quick wipe with 60 percent alcohol kills most of it on the spot.

items.name: Disposal bags
items.fact: With no bathroom to step into, there's nowhere to discreetly deal with a used pad or the like — sealing it away is what keeps that private.

items.name: Storage bags
items.fact: A lost ID or ruined papers can shut the door to shelter, benefits and work. A few bags with zip tops can keep things easy to access and protected from anything in or outside your bag or pocket.

items.name: Moleskin blister pads
items.fact: Blisters form from simple friction, and left unprotected they tear, sting and can get infected; a small bandage takes some of that rubbing for you.

items.name: Reusable totes
items.fact: Handed anything with a full pack already on your back, you make trips or leave some behind — one that folds to pocket size is there for the overflow and gone after.

items.name: Long sleeve shirts
items.fact: A layer against the skin traps a film of still air — one of the best insulators there is — and holds in the heat bare skin just gives away.

items.name: Neck gaiters
items.fact: Cold strips heat away from your neck and face as some of the first places on your body. A cover, when out in the elements, can minimize that heat loss.

items.name: Flashlights
items.fact: Finding your way, finding what you dropped in the dark, making sure a car sees you — few things you carry are as versatile as a beam of light.

items.name: AAA batteries
items.fact: Cold runs a cell down fast, and the light or alarm you're counting on is only as alive as its spares.

items.name: Whistles
items.fact: A shout gives out fast and doesn't carry, especially in wind; a whistle's sound travels much farther on a fraction of the breath, to call for help or warn someone off.

items.name: Hand warmers
items.fact: Fingers lose feeling before the rest of you, and numb hands can't work a zipper or strike a lighter — a little heat hands those back.

items.name: Cough drops
items.fact: A cold's raw throat and cough drag on for days and steal the sleep it takes to shake them — a lozenge quiets both long enough to rest.

items.name: Pens
items.fact: Many resources still require filling out paperwork by hand. Having a reliable pen on you reduces time spent on the logistics of filling them out.

items.name: Notebooks
items.fact: On the street there's rarely a space that's your own — a blank page is one you can carry: to write a letter, work a thought out, or just have.

items.name: Mini notebooks
items.fact: For times when a phone isn't available for quick notes or an important number, having somewhere to put them down that fits in a pocket so they can be written down quick can prevent them from getting forgotten.
